Hi Margaret. A couple updates from HLB

On Sept. 24th at the next HLB meeting there will be a resolution to withdraw and transfer of Heritage
Land Bank parcel 6-057K, legally described as Tract B-5, Girdwood Industrial Park, Phase 2 and
generally located at the terminus of Bedrock Circle in Girdwood, from the Heritage Land Bank inventory to
the Real Estate Services general inventory and assignment of management authority to the Street
Maintenance Section for use by Girdwood Valley Service Area.

The HLB lands in the proposed ORCA subdivision have been platted. HLB staff are working with the
Girdwood Housing Committee on potential development of Tract 2 for community housing objectives.

Thanks! Tim

Attachments:       image001.png

Hello,

In support of the drafting of the 2027 HLB Work Plan, we are requesting the public send us photos they have taken of or on HLB land.
These photos will be used throughout the plan, including the cover. Please let us know who we should credit, and when/where the
photos were taken. We would love photos of landscapes, plants, wildlife, and people recreating (but please no faces). We prefer photos
from 2026, but historical photos are welcome too! Your help with this is much appreciated!

The Heritage Land Bank Advisory Commission will be holding a meeting on Thursday, September 24, 2026, at 1:30pm. This will be
a hybrid meeting with in-person, online, and telephone options.

To join online via Microsoft Teams click this link to enter the meeting.
To join via telephone call 907-519-0237 and use conference ID 987 366 530​#
Or join in-person at the Permit & Development Center, Conf. Room 170, 4700 Elmore Road, Anchorage, Alaska 99507. Follow green
signs from the main lobby to find the correct conference room.

The meeting agenda is available online here. This meeting has one action item and public hearing, and one work session. The action
item is regarding a proposed transfer of management authority of HLB Pacel 6-057K, located in the Girdwood Industrial Park, to the
MOA Street Maintenance Section for use by the Girdwood Valley Service Area (public hearing notice). The work session is regarding the
drafting of the 2027 Work Plan. This is a conversation between staff and commissioners to get initial feedback on key updates and
proposals for the Work Plan. We are not accepting public comments on the Work Plan at this time. A comment period and public hearing
have not been scheduled but will be announced to this mailing list in the future. A draft of the work plan is not available at this time.

Community members may provide public comment during public hearings or Items or Persons Not on the Agenda. Anyone wishing to
provide public comment via email, telephone or Teams must email hlb@anchorageak.gov by 5:00 pm the day before the meeting.
In the email, please provide your name, phone number, and the subject line should read “HLBAC Public Comment.” All members of the
public on the Teams Meeting shall be muted until called on to speak. Those wishing to speak in-person do not need to sign up prior to the
meeting. Should you need additional assistance or special modifications to participate, or if you have questions, please call the HLB
office at 343-7536 or email hlb@anchorageak.gov.

More information will be posted on our website and sent out to our mailing list on August 14th. Please feel free to reach out with any
questions. Thank you!

Dear Planning Staﬀ:

Mt. Alyeska Ski Resort Limited Partnership, through its representa$ve Seth Andersen, submits this
Administra$ve Site Plan Review applica$on for the proposed six-plex at Alyeska Daylodge Subdivision,
Tract A.

Project Summary

The subject property is a 1.5-acre parcel recently created by Pla5ng Case S12721 and zoned GRST-1. The
overall development consists of:

    •  An exis$ng three-story, four-unit building, permi8ed under MOA Permit C25-1978 and currently
       under construc$on; and

    •  A proposed three-story, six-unit building.

The completed development will contain 10 dwelling units on 1.5 acres, resul$ng in a density of:

10 units ÷ 1.5 acres = 6.67 DUA.

The 6.67 DUA density places the development within the 4–8 DUA mul$ple-family dwelling category
iden$ﬁed in AMC Table 21.09-2, Table of Allowed Uses, which requires Administra$ve Site Plan Review in
the GRST-1 district.

The purpose of this applica$on is to obtain the required Municipality of Anchorage Land
Use/Administra$ve Site Plan approval for the proposed six-plex.

Previously Approved Site Development

The proposed six-plex is part of the overall site development previously reviewed by the Municipality.

The four-plex was approved under MOA Permit C25-1978. The approved plot plan, civil site plan, and
drainage plan depict the overall development, including the four-plex, proposed six-plex, site access,
grading, drainage, u$li$es, and associated site improvements.

Those approved plans are included with this applica$on as suppor$ng documenta$on.

The current applica$on does not propose a new site development conﬁgura$on. The proposed six-plex
follows the overall site plan previously reviewed in connec$on with C25-1978.

The combined four-plex and six-plex contain approximately 14,889 square feet of gross ﬂoor area, below
the applicable 20,000-square-foot threshold iden$ﬁed in the GRST-1 provisions for development master
planning.

Exis ng Permits and Agency Approvals

The site and proposed development have been subject to review by the Municipality and applicable
State and federal agencies. Approvals include:

Municipality of Anchorage

    •   C25-1978 – Land Use and Clear and Grub permit for the four-plex;

    •   C25-1877 – Clear and Grub permit associated with the six-plex;

    •   Fire Department Access approval; and

    •  Watershed Management sign-oﬀs associated with C25-1978 and C25-1877.

State of Alaska Fire Marshal

    •   Fire, Life Safety, and Engineering approvals under permits 2026ANCH0032 and 2026ANCH0033.

U.S. Army Corps of Engineers

    •   Permit POA-2025-00466 for work involving exis$ng culverts and realignment of an unnamed
        tributary of Glacier Creek.

Alaska Department of Fish and Game

    •   Fish Habitat Permit FH25-II-0112; and

    •  Aqua$c Resource Permit SF2025-191.

Alaska Department of Environmental Conserva on

    •  Storm Water Pollu$on Preven$on Plan Permit AKR10H0MH.

Anchorage Water and Wastewater U  lity

    •  Sewer main extension project S25-005; and

    •   Applicable onsite water and sewer permits.

The six-plex has received the applicable Fire Marshal access and ﬁll and grade approvals and the
iden$ﬁed State, federal, environmental, and u$lity approvals. The remaining approval addressed by this
applica$on is the Municipality of Anchorage Land Use/Administra$ve Site Plan approval.

Administra ve Site Plan Review Criteria

1. Consistency with Previously Approved Plans and Land Use Approvals

The proposed development is consistent with the Alyeska Daylodge Subdivision plat and previously
approved site development.

As shown on the approved C25-1978 plot plan, civil site plan, and drainage plan submi8ed with this
applica$on, the overall site conﬁgura$on includes both the permi8ed four-plex and proposed six-plex,
together with the associated site access, grading, drainage, u$lity, and other improvements.

The proposed six-plex therefore implements the overall site conﬁgura$on previously reviewed by the
Municipality rather than establishing a substan$ally diﬀerent development plan.

The project is also consistent with the 2024 Alyeska Resort Area Master Plan, approved by the
Municipality of Anchorage. The plan establishes a planning framework for the Alyeska Resort area,
including residen$al and commercial uses.

2. Compliance with Applicable Development and Design Standards

The project complies with the applicable GRST-1 development and design standards.

Use and Density. The proposed use is mul$ple-family dwelling at 4–8 DUA, an allowed use subject to
Administra$ve Site Plan Review under AMC Table 21.09-2, Table of Allowed Uses. The completed
development will contain 10 units at 6.67 DUA.

Zoning District. The proposed residen$al development is consistent with the intent and established
character of the GRST-1 district and the Alyeska Resort base area.

Dimensional Standards. The development complies with the applicable GRST-1 dimensional standards in
Table 21.09-8. Applicable dimensions are shown on the submi8ed site and architectural plans.

Hazard Areas. The site is not located within a high-hazard avalanche or rockfall area and does not
contain slopes exceeding 35 percent.

Grading and Drainage. The civil plans maintain exis$ng drainage pa8erns and provide controlled
drainage through exis$ng drainage features and onsite swales. Previously approved culvert replacement
and channel realignment improvements are incorporated into the site development.

Landscaping and Vegeta on. The buildings are located primarily on exis$ng gravel parking areas,
minimizing disturbance to natural vegeta$on. Exis$ng vegeta$on exceeds 20 percent of the site and
permeable surfaces exceed 40 percent. Exis$ng vegeta$on within required setbacks will generally be
maintained. Previously approved stream and culvert improvements are the principal excep$ons.

Transporta on and Access. No new streets are proposed. Access is provided from the exis$ng road
system, with driveway improvements shown on the civil plans.

Pedestrian Connec  vity. Walkways connect the residen$al buildings, parking areas, entrances, and
adjacent right-of-way.

U  li  es. Water, sewer, and other u$lity improvements are coordinated with the applicable u$lity
providers and will comply with applicable requirements.

Snow Management. Snow storage is provided on the civil plans and exceeds 20 percent of the total
plowed area. Snow storage areas are located outside required natural vegeta$on areas and provide
posi$ve drainage away from structures and pavement.

Parking. Parking and vehicle circula$on are shown on the civil site plan. The garage conﬁgura$on
complies with the applicable standards for mul$family parking located below or par$ally below grade.

Signage. No commercial or project iden$ﬁca$on signage is proposed. Building signage is limited to
addressing.

Driveway. The driveway and site access improvements shown on the civil plans comply with the
applicable driveway standards.

Exterior Materials, Color and Textures. Exterior siding is proposed to be standing seam metal siding of a
dark color with ma8e sheen. There will be accents of natural wood. Rooﬁng will be a combina$on of
asphalt shingles and EPDM rubber rooﬁng at low slope roofs.

3. Signiﬁcant Adverse Impacts

The project is not an$cipated to result in signiﬁcant adverse impacts.

The site is an established gravel parking area, allowing the proposed buildings to be located with limited
disturbance to natural vegeta$on. Exis$ng drainage pa8erns are maintained or improved, and addi$onal
vegetated and permeable areas will support inﬁltra$on and surface-water treatment.

The exis$ng steep site access is being replaced with an improved driveway loca$on and grade.

Previously approved improvements to the unnamed tributaries of Glacier Creek include replacement of
exis$ng perched culvert outlets with shorter and shallower culverts and channel improvements intended
to improve ﬁsh passage and aqua$c habitat.

These measures minimize poten$al impacts associated with drainage, access, vegeta$on, and stream
crossings.

4. Comprehensive Plan Consistency

The project is consistent with the 2025 Girdwood Comprehensive Plan and the 2024 Alyeska Resort Area
Master Plan.

The property's land use designa$on is Mixed-Use, which accommodates residen$al and commercial
uses. The surrounding Alyeska Resort base area contains established resort, commercial, and residen$al
uses.

The proposed six-plex adds residen$al housing within this established mixed-use and resort environment
and supports housing needs associated with the Alyeska Resort area.

Conclusion

The proposed six-plex is the second building iden$ﬁed in the overall site development previously
reviewed by the Municipality in connec$on with MOA Permit C25-1978.

The approved C25-1978 plot plan, civil site plan, and drainage plan, submi8ed with this applica$on,
document the previously reviewed overall site conﬁgura$on.

The completed development will contain 10 dwelling units on 1.5 acres, resul$ng in 6.67 DUA and
placing the project within the 4–8 DUA mul$ple-family dwelling category requiring Administra$ve Site
Plan Review under AMC Table 21.09-2.

The project complies with the applicable development and design standards, incorporates previously
approved site and environmental improvements, and is consistent with the applicable comprehensive
and area master plans.

The applicant respecJully requests approval of the Administra$ve Site Plan Review and associated
Municipality of Anchorage Land Use approval for the proposed six-plex.

                            Roads and Drainages
Road Status: As we move further into fall, we’re trying to wrap up summer maintenance, with
several small projects still to complete. Recently, we completed drainage improvements on Old
Dawson and Gold in Old Town, including digging out the drainages on both streets, lowering 2
culverts on Dawson, and replacing two culverts on Gold. We added recycled pavement asphalt
(RAP) to both roads and driveway approaches to bring up the grade for improved drainage and
add more protection to the driveway culverts.  Western crack-sealed all paved roads and parking
lots under GVSA management this past month.  I took the opportunity to get 400 yards of asphalt
millings from the Granite Construction Seward Highway project at a very good price of $24.50 a
yard, delivered to the GVSA stockpile, which we will use as RAP for gravel road improvement
projects. We hope to get more when they return to pave later this month. This material works
well to increase the strength of dirt roads. We opened bids for the winter gravel purchase of
1200 Tons, and Northern Gravel was the only bidder, with a winning bid of $72,000.00, or $60
per ton delivered to the GVSA Yard. We will take delivery of it later this month. As we move
further into fall and winter, we will transition to winter operations, and Western will get the
equipment ready for that.

                           Major project updates:
Ruane Road fish passage culvert replacement. The Boutet company will lead project
management for this new culvert project, and the Jacobs company will help ensure compliance
with the EPA grant and federal requirements. EPA has approved our Request for Proposal
(RFP) for Design and Engineering services for the new culvert. The committee selected HDR
Engineering, Inc. to provide design and engineering services and prepare bid documents for
construction of the new culvert. Negotiations are currently underway with HDR to sign a
contract. Design and engineering should start this fall and into winter.

Winner Creek Trail Bridge at the Glacier Creek crossing: A contract has been signed with
Spernak and Sons for them to procure the bridge construction materials and build the bridge. We
have a pre-construction meeting with the contractor this week to kick off the project and confirm
the construction schedule. This project will start this summer and be completed next summer in
2027. The materials needed for this project have long lead times, and recent disruptions in
global markets have led to unforeseen increases in material, freight, and fuel costs. Besides the
challenges this project already faces because of its location, these unforeseen market conditions
only add more work to complete this great bridge for the community. The contractor is making
steps forward to fully start the project next spring, with completion by the end of summer 2027.

GVSA Road Maintenance contract: The bids have been opened on the new GVSA road
maintenance contract for 2026-2031, and Western Construction was the only bidder to win it
with a total bid of $1,117,875.00. A memo recommending award to Western has been sent to the
MOA purchasing department. The contract will require Assembly approval as a consent agenda
item at their next regular meeting on October 6th. The new contract will be a 5-year term
contract with two options to extend for two (2) additional two (2) year renewals.

Subject:  Architectural Code Study and Gravity Load Analysis of the
             Little Bears Daycare Building (Girdwood Community Center)

Dear Mr. Huzey:

Per your request, USKH Inc. (USKH) performed an architectural code study and gravity load analysis of
the Little Bears Daycare building in Girdwood. Additionally, we have computed a rough order of
magnitude (ROM) cost estimate to repair the building’s structural and architectural deficiencies, and
have also prepared a ROM cost estimate for a completely new building. A site visit was conducted by
two engineers from USKH on Thursday, May 12, 2011. During the site visit, the engineers measured
the overall dimensions of the building, examined roof and crawlspace cavities, and as-built enough of
the building to perform the code study and structural analysis. The code study and structural analysis
was not all-inclusive, and there may be hidden or other building deficiencies. Electrical and mechanical
reviews were excluded from the scope and not performed. An ADA review was also excluded. The
building might have significant mechanical and/or electrical needs that have not been covered in the
estimate. The building was evaluated against code requirements (2006 IBC as amended by the
Municipality of Anchorage) for the apparent actual occupancy.

Building Description

The building is located in Girdwood, Alaska at the intersection of the Alyeska Highway and Hightower
Road. The building is L-shaped with a small lean-to build out for the front entry, and a small canopy
with wood stairs to the rear. The approximate building dimensions are 60-feet (ft) long and 24-ft wide
for the main wing and 24-ft by 24-ft for the L wing. The building height is approximately 12 ft, and it has
an area of 2,100 square feet. A large canopy spans between this building and the adjacent Glacier City
Hall building. The large canopy is covered in the Glacier City Hall report. The main wing of the building
is completely open with a vaulted ceiling. The L wing is broken up into a small kitchen, office,
restrooms, utility room, and storage area. The building is wood framed with a concrete foundation and
crawlspace. Attic and crawlspace access are located in the storage room.

The roof is framed with 2 x 8 inch rafters spaced at 24 inches on center (o.c.). Along the rafters span 1
x 10 inch members, and metal roofing is attached to these members. At the southeast corner of the
building adjacent to the large canopy, the roof is shingled. At this location plywood decking is installed
over the 1x10 members, with the shingles and underlayment applied to the plywood. The shingled area
represents approximately 25 percent of the total roof. The ceiling is supported with 2 x 8 inch ceiling
joists spaced at 24 inches o.c. The floor is framed with 2 x 8 inch joists spaced at 16 inches o.c. The
joists span from the exterior concrete foundation to an interior multi-ply beam composed of three 2 x 8
inch members. All of the lumber appeared to be a fir grade.

Gravity Load Analysis

The structural analysis was limited to gravity only and wind and seismic loads were not considered. The
snow load considered was a flat roof snow load of 120 pounds per square foot (psf). This loading is
identical to the loading used for the new Girdwood Post Office building not far from the site. Since this
building has a framed floor, the maximum effect from an overall live load of 40 psf, or 1,000 pound point
load, was considered. This matches the code-required live load considerations for school occupancies.

The results of the analysis show that the roof rafters have a demand/capacity ratio in excess of 3. This
means the required strength per code-prescribed loads is over 3 times the actual computed strength.
The floor joists are adequate for a uniform 40 psf load, but not for the 1,000 pound point load.
Conversely, the floor beams are adequate for the point load, but not the uniform load. We conclude the
roof framing is not adequate to support the required loads by a large margin. We also conclude the floor
framing is not adequate for the two live load conditions required for a school occupancy.

Based on previous experience with similar buildings, a combination of two factors has likely kept the
roof from failing. The roof is mostly composed of metal sheets without any wood sheathing and the attic
is not well insulated. We surmise heat is escaping into the attic space through the light insulation and
directly heats the metal roofing, which is mostly exposed in the attic. This allows the snow to melt
and/or slide off the roof, relieving snow load before it can build up. Visual observation of the roof
confirms the intersection between the two wings of the building (valley line) has noticeable permanent
deflection. The valley line bows instead of being straight. This area is expected to accumulate snow
more than the other areas of the roof.

Floor live load limit is a statutory limit given in the building code. The actual observed load is much
lower. The daycare space was mostly open, with only some small bookshelves and furniture. Normal
daily activities in this area will not overload the floor. The floor loading may be an issue in the storage
and utility rooms. In these rooms, there are shelves loaded with heavy blocks and a washer, dryer, and
water heater. The occupants should be aware of the floor live load capacity in the storage room to
avoid overloading.

We recommend the building remain unoccupied during winter months until the roof framing is retrofitted
for the prescribed snow load. The building may be occupied this summer until the first snowfall. Care
should be taken to avoid overloading the floor in the storage and utility areas.

Architectural Code Study

The building is classified by local amendment as occupancy type Group E, Educational. This is the
required classification for a daycare. The actual type of construction is Type V-B, which is defined as
any type of construction for structural elements, interior, and exterior walls of any type of materials
permitted by the code. This type of construction does not have a particular fire-resistance rating nor is a
sprinkler system provided. Smoke detectors and fire extinguishers were present in several areas of the
building. A manual fire alarm system was also present with several pull stations throughout the building.
It is not known if the smoke detectors were combination CO detectors; this should be verified. The
building is heated with gas-fired, direct vent unit heaters. CO detectors are required per local
amendment due to these combustion devices. A ventilation system was added but it unclear whether
the controls are by manual or automatic operation.

The local amendments require a sprinkler system for Group E occupancies except when used as a
daycare and 49 or less occupants. This provides an absolute maximum occupancy since no sprinkler
system is provided. The allowable building height and building area appears within the limits given in
the code. The maximum occupant load based on the classification and building area is 48 occupants,
which is less than the absolute maximum via local amendment; therefore 48 occupants is the maximum
allowed. During the site visit, this occupancy was not observed to be exceeded. Egress travel and the
number of exits conform to the code requirements. There are some deficiencies regarding incidental
use areas and egress, however. The L Wing has a laundry room and storage area over 100 square
feet. This area must be separated by 1 hour construction from the main occupancy. The walls appear to
be standard residential construction (wood studs, ½-inch gypsum wall board) and no fire rated door is
provided to separate the spaces. The rear egress door has a large glass panel which does not appear
to be safety glass. Additionally, there is a window within a few inches of this egress door which is also
not safety glass. The exits are identified with signs, but there is no emergency illumination for either
exit.

The building is in close proximity to the adjacent Glacier City Hall building. The code requires a
minimum separation depending on the occupancy type and level of fire-resistive construction. Since
both buildings are on the same lot, a code provision is triggered which effectively reduces the actual
separation distance by half. The result is that a one-hour rated exterior wall assembly is required on the
side of the building facing the adjacent building. A parapet would also need to extend from the roof. The
canopy spanning between the two buildings is not fire rated and would need to be removed.

Recommended Improvements

The recommended improvements to bring the building to a minimum life-safety code level for structural
and architectural are:

    •  Remove entire roof and re-frame with adequately designed trusses and roof sheathing.
    •  Reconstruct wall facing Glacier City Hall building into 1-hour rated wall with parapet.
    •  Add supports in crawlspace to brace floor.
    •  Add wood shear walls, hold downs, and foundation anchors to resist lateral forces.
    •  Provide egress illumination.
    •  Replace rear exit door.
    •  Replace glazing adjacent to rear exit door with safety glass.
    •  Add code-compliant handrail and balusters to side exit exterior stair.
    •  Reconstruct and/or patch roofing, finishes, mechanical, and electrical for new work.
    •   Verify CO detection or provide detectors.
    •  Post maximum occupant load sign of 48 occupants.

This is in regards to Crews’s proposed Resolution for Transparency Around Bed Tax Earnings
and Expenses from the August meeting. Summary of that effort: get muni to publish better data
on where, how, and when bed tax is earned and spent.

In the last few days, Nick Crews met with GVSA manager Kyle Kelly and GBOS co-chair
Jennifer Wingard to review Crews’s initial proposal. Out of those meetings, we had some
conclusions.

     -   Split this into two different efforts, earning and spending. They involve different parties at
       the muni (eg visit anchorage deals with spending but not earning), and the efforts don’t
      depend on each other, so we can make progress on one without being slowed down by
       the other.
     -  The muni is probably aligned in many ways with us, eg they also want to understand
      where geographically the bed tax is coming from. So we should be collaborative at first
      and not just demand things of them.
     -   Instead of asking for a resolution from GBOS now, Nick will first shop these proposals
      around with the muni parties to get feedback, edits, buy in, and to hopefully find allies.
     -   Nick will report back to GBOS at the Oct meeting.

Income Transparency

     -   Per-unit bed tax income is going to be very difficult to get. It is not available to the
        municipality. Airbnb delivers the owed tax to the muni in one big lump sum. If we want
        per-unit income info, then the muni would have to request airbnb to report it. Airbnb
       already rejected this request once, and they probably have the legal ground to stand on:
        In 2019 a federal judge ruled that airbnb did not have to comply with NYC’s demand for
        per-unit data [1]
     -  Pre-aggregated data may be feasible. In 2024, AO 2024-81(S) requird hosting
       platforms such as Airbnb and VRBO to submit additional data to the Municipality
       alongside the platforms’ tax returns. Hosting platforms are required to report the total
      number of operators included in the tax return and details about the type of lodging
       provided, such as location and unit type by month. It feels like a small step to require
      zipcode information as well.
               -   This zipcode-level data will not help Girdwood answer policy questions around
          STRs that well (would need unit-level data for that), but will help Girdwood argue
                 for our share of the Bed Tax spending, eg TIPS, EMS, etc
     -  Nick will attempt to meet, within the next month, with assembly member Zac
      Johnson, and someone from the administration. We need a code change for the
      muni to be able to force airbnb to release this. If others wish to be part of these

meetings, please email Nick.


Spending Transparency
     -  Nick will attempt to meet, within the next month, with Visit Anchorage and the
      muni’s budget department. Perhaps they do already know where the money is being
       spent, it just isn’t published. Will try to find a path forward so that neighborhoods can
       understand how much of the bed tax money is going to them. Only if they are not helpful
       should we attempt to go above them and get help from the mayor or assembly. If others
       wish to be part of these meetings, please email Nick.

The following information addresses specific organization of the Girdwood Board of

Article 1: MEMBERSHIP.

   A. The GBOS shall consist of five (5) elected Members.

B. The elected Members are elected officials, thus subject to the MOA laws
       governing removal from office. Generally stated:

         Meeting Absences: A Member intending to be absent at a Regular Meeting
            shall request from the Chair or Co-Chair to be excused in advance of the
          meeting from which he will be absent. Vacancy of a seat shall occur on the
            failure of a Member to
                    1. Attend three (3) consecutive Regular or Special Meetings or Work
                   Sessions without an excused absence from the Chair or Co-Chair;
                 2. Attend a two-thirds (2/3) majority of the Regular and Special Meetings,
             Work Sessions, Executive Sessions and GBOS Public Hearings during
                any calendar year without an excused absences from the Chair or Co
                  Chair.
          Recall Procedure: GBOS will follow MOA guidelines for any potential recall
           of a GBOS member.
          Resignation by a member: Member shall submit a signed letter of resignation
            to the Chair or Co-Chair and to the Mayor concurrently.
                         .

            Filling the vacancy will be done in accordance with MOA code in the
          following manner:
                  1. Public notice of seat vacancy will be posted for a minimum of fourteen
                   (14) full days stating specific Seat Vacant, Term, and requesting that a
                    brief resume from those interested in filling the seat be submitted to the
                                  GBOS by a specified closing date.
                 2. Within seven (7) days of the closing date for resumes, the GBOS will
                meet in Executive Session to make a recommendation to be forwarded
                    to the Mayor.
                 3. The Mayor will then make an appointment to fill out the term of the
                    seat left vacant.

Article 2: COMMITTEES.
   The Girdwood Board of Supervisors has established the following Standing
   Committees:

   A. Land Use Committee: There shall be a Land Use Committee (hereafter “LUC”)
      which shall function as an advisory committee to the GBOS on all Girdwood Land
      Use issues. The LUC shall operate in accordance with the Girdwood Land Use
      Committee Operating Principles as approved by the LUC and amended as needed.

      The LUC is a one-person one-vote organization, whereas GBOS business is voted
      upon by only the 5 board members. In consort with the ideals of community
       councils being the voice of the people with one-person one-vote, the LUC is
       designated by the GBOS to be the public hearing process for the GBOS. In the
       event that the voting in LUC and GBOS do not match each other, the rules under
      Voting Conclusions, Article 6, Section E will be followed.

          It is intended that, on all matters involving Conditional Use Permits, Vacation
       Applications and Easement Applications the LUC will “hear” the matter first, and
        then, in accordance with the GBOS policies for these items, will send forward to
       the GBOS its recommendations and/or vote on the matter. Once the LUC has sent
       forward to the GBOS its recommendations on a given matter, that matter may then
      be put on the next available GBOS agenda for GBOS discussion, vote and action
       or recommendation to the appropriate MOA department or authority. All  effort
        shall be made for Girdwood land use type issues to be heard before the LUC first
      and voted upon by members. In situations with time constraints that preclude prior
       hearings at LUC, such issues will be heard by GBOS and  their recommendation
        will be forwarded  to the appropriate authority, with  the caveat that time did not
       permit the issue to be heard and voted upon by the LUC.

   B. Trails Committee: Given the importance of local and regional trails in the Girdwood
        valley, there shall be a Trails Committee which shall function as an  advisory
      committee to the GBOS on all matters related to trails in the Girdwood valley. The
        Trails Committee shall operate in accordance with procedures  adopted by the
      Committee, approved by the GBOS and amended as needed.

   C. Public Safety Advisory Committee: The Public Safety Advisory Committee
      (PSAC) shall function as an advisory committee to the GBOS in all matters related
        to policing and public safety in the Girdwood valley. The PSAC  shall operate in
       accordance with procedures adopted by the Committee, approved by the GBOS and
      amended as needed.

   D. Girdwood Housing and Economic Committee: The Girdwood Housing and
      Economic Committee (GHEC) shall function as an advisory committee to the
    GBOS in all matters related to housing, development, and economic stability in the
     GVSA.The GHEC shall operate in accordance with procedures adopted by the
      Committee, approved by th GBOS, and amended as needed.

       the time set for meeting.

Article 6: VOTING.

A. Conflict ofInterest: A Member shall disclose any private interest that may create a
